claims.claim_text: Component distributors opened programmatic access to their part databases because EDA tool vendors were building parametric search and pricing into design software and needed to query that data directly; a distributor that kept its database closed risked being routed around.
claims.quote_verbatim: we have to give access to our database. Otherwise, we're going to fall behind and go out of business
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Layouts and Design-Outs

claims.claim_text: Google's Android Development Kit, announced at Google I/O in 2011, defined an API for an Android phone to talk over USB, with Bluetooth planned later, to an attached Arduino-class board, positioning the phone as the display and control surface for external hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a defined API to talk through the USB interface for now, possibly Bluetooth in the future, down to this Arduino board
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer and Jeremy Blum - Audacious Arduino Arguments

claims.claim_text: The Arduino 1.0 release changed the core API, and a substantial body of existing third-party sketches and libraries would no longer compile against it.
claims.quote_verbatim: They've changed the API, the application programming interface. Presumably for good reasons. In the future, everyone will thank them for it, right? But at the moment, no, a lot of the existing code out there is broken
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Otiose Ontocyclic Opiniasters

claims.claim_text: Where an ecosystem's principal asset is its accumulated body of example code, a breaking API change devalues that asset even when the per-file fix is trivial: a beginner following an old example gets a compile failure reported as cryptic C++ errors rather than a statement that the code targets an older API.
claims.quote_verbatim: is incompatible with the new API. It's not hard, apparently, to change the code to fix it. But the fact is, you know, if you're a beginner, you download it, compile, fail, doesn't work. Gives you all these cryptic C++ error messages
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Otiose Ontocyclic Opiniasters

claims.claim_text: Ettus Research publishes a single driver, the USRP Hardware Driver (UHD), and exposes one API to all users; the LabVIEW drivers written with National Instruments, the MathWorks MATLAB and Simulink drivers, and GNU Radio all build on that same API rather than each talking to the hardware directly.
claims.quote_verbatim: we give everybody the same API, national instruments builds on top of it
claims.speaker: Matt Ettus
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Ettus - Quality Quadrature Quidam

claims.claim_text: A common driver API across a product family means application code does not change when the user moves between devices in that family; the vendor absorbs the device-specific handling inside the driver.
claims.quote_verbatim: it doesn't matter which of our hardware devices you use. It has the same UHD API
claims.speaker: Matt Ettus
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Ettus - Quality Quadrature Quidam

claims.claim_text: castAR planned not to conceal the LED modulation scheme used for tracking, and to ship APIs and a prototyping system alongside the product so that third parties could build their own tracked objects and applications, including uses outside gaming such as surgical simulators and teaching aids.
claims.quote_verbatim: We want to provide the APIs and the prototyping system. So, if you want to just experiment with the prototyping system, you can make your own game experiences that way
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: The I2Cdev library is structured as a base class that performs raw I2C transfers of a bit, a byte or a string of bytes in a single call, with per-device classes layered on top of it; the device class for a part such as the MPU-6050 does the register-level work so the application receives orientation data directly in a chosen format.
claims.quote_verbatim: the I2C dev base class. And then there's device classes built on top of that, that, that, uh, make use of those functions
claims.speaker: Jeff Rowberg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Rowberg - Mini Module Master

claims.claim_text: Upverter assembled its component data from several sources at once: Octopart's API, described as the best publicly available API data, supplemented by direct feeds negotiated with distributors including DigiKey, Arrow, Newark and Mouser, and by direct arrangements with semiconductor vendors including TI and Freescale.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's kind of the best publicly available API data that's out there. Um, and, and they're working to make it a lot better. And that's, that's a really good thing for both them and us. Um, but we also work with DigiKey and Arrow and Newark and Mouser, um, to get data more directly, um, from distributors. And then we're also working with the semiconductor guys. So we're working with TI and Freescale and a couple other, um, big semiconductor guys to get data directly from them
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: Pebble exposed the watch's Bluetooth connection state to third-party application developers through its SDK, so an app could report to the user whether the watch was still in range of the phone.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've made that available as an API to some app developers
claims.speaker: Andrew Witte
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: A CAD tool whose component library is backed by the Octopart API could not create a part that did not already exist in that upstream database, so the tool's part coverage was bounded by the data provider's coverage.
claims.quote_verbatim: that uses Octopart API in the back end. Yeah, that's right. Just can you make it without having access to Octopart? They said you can't make a new component
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Get Smart About Automation - Caducous Cyborg Concerns

claims.claim_text: A product built on a third party's connectivity service inherits that supplier's freedom to change its API or to be acquired by an owner with different intentions; either event propagates to every unit already in the field.
claims.quote_verbatim: Electric Imp tomorrow could change their API, you know, and how that stuff happens. And it's like, if it doesn't ripple through the chain
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Warming Up To IoT - Tendentious Thermal Tools

claims.claim_text: Interface documentation is part of the interface: a well-documented API, whether on a web service or on a hardware component, is a selection criterion in its own right because it determines how quickly an integrator can get working without reinventing existing functionality.
claims.quote_verbatim: an internet service that has this excellently documented API, you know, that, that's such a draw for me because I really rely on that. Same with hardware
claims.speaker: Matt Richardson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Richardson - Raspberry Risorgimento Regent

claims.claim_text: Amazon Mechanical Turk's API lets the requester set the price attached to each task, and that price sets the latency: roughly ten to fifteen minutes at ten cents a job, about ten minutes at twenty-five cents, and seconds at around two dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: the API lets you put any price you want on the job. So if I put 10 cents on a job, it would be about 10 to 15 minutes. I put 25 cents on a job. It would be maybe 10 minutes. When I was demoing it for my instructor, I put about $2 on the job and got it done in a matter of seconds
claims.speaker: Matt Richardson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Richardson - Raspberry Risorgimento Regent

claims.claim_text: MacroFab built each capability as an API first and layered the user interface on top of it, with the work split across a microservice backend; on that division the user interface accounted for a small share of development effort compared with the models and controllers behind it.
claims.quote_verbatim: we take sort of an API first approach. So we start with an API for any capability and then we put the UI on top of that
claims.speaker: Chris Church
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: Cloud back ends behind device APIs fail more often than device makers expect, and the outage is not signalled to the operator, so every deployed unit can stop receiving data before anyone is aware of it.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of these servers, they go down quite frequently. And the problem is you don't know almost immediately if it happens
claims.speaker: Luke Beno
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Luke Beno of Analog.io

claims.claim_text: When a cloud service revises its API, shipped appliances that embed a client for it lose the function until their firmware is updated, as when a networked refrigerator could no longer sign in to a calendar service.
claims.quote_verbatim: your fridge needs a software update to use the new API
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Our Second Callin Show(ish)

claims.claim_text: Home automation integration is per-device work: each bulb or appliance is commissioned separately and exposes its own API, so third-party software in that space exists largely to bind those separate APIs together in the absence of a common standard.
claims.quote_verbatim: each light bulb you have to set up independently. Each device you have to set up independently. And then they all have APIs that you have to tie into
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Artificially Intelligent Party Platform

claims.claim_text: In large LED installation work the controller supplier defines the control API rather than accepting the integrator's, specifying the packet format and the send sequence and keeping the link one-way; with no return path there is no error handling to implement or to get wrong.
claims.quote_verbatim: I give them the API. So here's the packet format. Here's the send. It's generally very simple. It's almost always one way. Just keep things simple
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: Live from Serbia with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Opening a device-level API on a mass-market product is in tension with being a viable consumer product: a small number of users exercise it productively while a larger number render units unusable.
claims.quote_verbatim: i would like to open up the api to the devices on the device level and give everyone access to everything but guess what you know a couple of people will do it a couple of people will enjoy using it but most people will brick it
claims.speaker: Omer Kilic
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Omer Kilic

claims.claim_text: The cost of an open device-level API is not the engineering but the support structure behind it; for a product installed in a wall, the RMA path itself is expensive, and a six-person team cannot carry that load.
claims.quote_verbatim: building the support network and the rma process for in wall you know live devices
claims.speaker: Omer Kilic
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Omer Kilic

claims.claim_text: Third-party integration with a connected product was planned at the API level, preferably on the local network rather than through the cloud, instead of by shipping a C++ SDK, so that integrators are not bound to one implementation language.
claims.quote_verbatim: i'm not just gonna give people a c++ sdk and let them write code it's gonna be a process where they can pick whatever language they want
claims.speaker: Omer Kilic
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Omer Kilic

claims.claim_text: MacroFab exposes an API endpoint for every function of its web application, so a customer's own web store can trigger fulfilment of an order against inventory held at the contract manufacturer without a human placing the build request.
claims.quote_verbatim: everything is also uh has an api endpoint so you can write your own software if you want to to also interface with your
claims.episode_title: Mashuppery (with MEP)

claims.claim_text: Appliance manufacturers including GE, Samsung and Belkin published device APIs into the IFTTT service, making a third-party aggregator the practical integration point for conditional automation between products from different vendors; the result is a common service rather than a standard.
claims.quote_verbatim: GE put a bunch of their like devices on there. You know, they publish APIs towards their washing machine or whatever. Like if, if washing machine done, then. Yeah. Then send email or then call phone
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Mapping Out Nerdery

claims.claim_text: A Wi-Fi sensor node spends multiple seconds waking, associating and transmitting before returning to sleep, which dominates its energy budget; on the ESP8266 that wake time was judged reducible to a half or a third by changing a few SDK APIs.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you change a few APIs here and there, you can probably do this like in, in what half or maybe a third of the time
claims.speaker: Jeroen Domburg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeroen Domburg (Sprite_tm)

claims.claim_text: Exposing test hardware through an API does not remove the labour of using it: a skilled engineer still has to write the automated test against that API and wire it into the build pipeline that runs on code check-in, which keeps such a business engineering-services heavy rather than volume-hardware heavy.
claims.quote_verbatim: you still need a skilled engineer to figure out how to consume that API and like make an automated test for it
claims.speaker: Jason Huggins
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: Board bring-up documentation is usefully treated as an API for the hardware, stating for each pin what software may do with it and in which direction. Inferring direction from net names is unreliable: a net named with "out" may be an output of the peripheral and therefore an input to the processor.
claims.quote_verbatim: I want to know GPIOs, should they be inputs or outputs? Turned out I had an output because it said out. And so I naively thought that if the net name had the word out in it, it should be an output from my processor. But that wasn't true
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Pedantic or Andrantic

claims.claim_text: In LiteX-based FPGA designs a host bridge lets Python scripts on a PC read and write the Wishbone registers of peripherals instantiated inside the FPGA. With MicroPython running on a soft core the same scripts run on-chip unchanged, because the register API is identical and only the transport, bridge versus direct memory access, differs.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're writing to direct memory locations, but the API looks the same
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tim "Mithro" Ansell

claims.claim_text: A BeagleBone motion-control stack presented a stepper element with a move-to-position or move-by-increment call and isolated the PRU-specific code behind a hardware abstraction layer, so the same interface could be carried to other boards.
claims.quote_verbatim: they created a stepper element. Uh huh. And then they would send like an API, like to, it acts like an API and you say, move to position XYZ and it just does it. Or, or I guess. Yep. They just gave it incremental, like move this. Yeah. Move this. And yeah, they had a big, uh, what's it called? Their hardware extraction layer where they just, they separate the PRU from the hardware that way they moved towards other boards
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Kridner and Robert Nelson

claims.claim_text: CircuitPython factors the C code that implements its Python-visible API out of the individual hardware ports into one shared implementation, which then calls down into port-specific C; the objects exposed to Python are C structs. The shared layer is what makes the API uniform across chips.
claims.quote_verbatim: the API is shared, like the code that implements the API is shared. Um, so the, the way that circuit Python works under the hood is that it's all C code and there's just structs that represent objects that you can use from Python. And so what I did is I factored that out of all the ports and made, and therefore it's uniform across all of them. And then that code just calls other C code that is port specific
claims.speaker: Scott Shawcroft
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Shawcroft

claims.claim_text: MicroPython offers no guarantee that a script written against one port runs on another, so code written for an ESP8266 will not necessarily work on an STM32; portability has to be engineered into the API layer rather than assumed from a shared language.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you took the code from your 8266 and you tried to put it onto a STM 32 wouldn't necessarily work. In fact, probably wouldn't work. Yeah. Well, other way around. There was no guarantee
claims.speaker: Scott Shawcroft
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Shawcroft

claims.claim_text: Automation services such as IFTTT and Zapier are graphical front ends over vendor APIs. Writing directly against those APIs instead removes the intermediary but transfers the maintenance burden: the upstream API changes and the integration must be kept up to date.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're all talking to APIs, and they're kind of like nice GUIs on top of them. And, you know, a lot of the times, like the standard thing is like, oh, well, you know, use Python to just access this API, and I'm like, no. I don't feel good with that. Or to be honest, too, like the API changes underneath, and you have to kind of keep up on it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Sipping Coulombs

claims.claim_text: PartsBox is a web-based personal parts inventory that pulls component data from distributor APIs, so a physical drawer of stock can be searched by specification, by what was paid for it and by remaining quantity, replacing hand-written part numbers on drawer labels.
claims.quote_verbatim: they actually hit the DigiKey APIs or maybe the Octobar API or something like that and get all the part data for you
claims.speaker: Spencer Wright
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Spencer Wright

claims.claim_text: Before programmatic pricing, component quoting was done by emailing spreadsheets to several distributors, comparing the returned prices line by line, and splitting the bill of materials across suppliers where the saving justified the extra purchase orders; the work queued behind whatever one person could process in a day.
claims.quote_verbatim: You send it off to four different distributors. They're all getting spreadsheets. They send it back. You then say, Oh, well the best prices for components one through 10 are from distributor a and 12, 11 through 20 are from just distributor B
claims.speaker: Chris Denney
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: Instant assembly quoting from uploaded native EDA files became possible only once component price, location and stock could be queried programmatically; Octopart's API supplied that layer at the time services such as CircuitHub were being built.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to have some kind of electronic API that goes out and does all that. Well, the timing was right because you had companies like Octopart starting. They gave you an API to be able to determine how expensive all the parts are and where they were and whether they were in stock
claims.speaker: Chris Denney
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: An API reference that lists public functions without describing their behaviour leaves the porting engineer to discover the constraints by experiment: on the early ESP32 the documentation did not say which calls were safe from an interrupt or under the RTOS, which made porting into a multi-core, RTOS-based part substantially harder than the Arduino-level documentation suggested.
claims.quote_verbatim: some of the things that aren't documented are what works in interrupts, what works in the RTOS, what doesn't, uh, the API, um, has, you know, the, uh, public functions defined, but what's going on behind the scenes
claims.speaker: Bart Dring
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bart Dring

claims.claim_text: A certified wireless module ships with a vendor-supplied API, often no more than AT commands, which transfers responsibility for the radio's correctness and its field testing to the module supplier. A wired link such as RS-485 has no equivalent pre-certified, pre-tested building block, so the integrator retains that testing work, which can make wireless the easier path to a reliable integration.
claims.quote_verbatim: the company has been as nice to make some kind of API for you, you know, even if it's just as simple as AT commands and that's all been done
claims.speaker: JP Norair
claims.episode_title: An Interview with JP Norair

claims.claim_text: Production programming and test tools frequently expose only a GUI and no API, so a factory cannot wrap them in a simplified operator interface; the operator wants a single go button with a green or red result, not a panel of a hundred and fifty controls that can be set wrongly.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of them don't even have any sort of API that they could, you know, just put a layer on top of it to abstract that away
claims.speaker: Jonathan Georgino
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Georgino

claims.claim_text: A hardware revision-control service integrates with PLM systems from outside by querying their APIs and using the component information already carried in the CAD design as the link between the two, since PLM systems draw on that same design data.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're a bit on the, the outside of those systems and just using the APIs for, um, for querying and basically using the design information in the CAD design as kind of like our liaison to the PLM systems, because they tend to pull that information from PLM
claims.speaker: Kyle Dumont
claims.episode_title: Hardware Revision Control with Kyle Dumont

claims.claim_text: A Zephyr device driver is written by populating a predefined struct for its device class with the required function pointers, such as initialisation, write and clear for a real-time clock; the application then obtains the device by name through the device tree and calls it as a generic device.
claims.quote_verbatim: all the functions get pushed into a struct, like a struct constructors, like what's your init function? What's your write time function? What's your clear time function
claims.speaker: Jared Wolff
claims.episode_title: Cellular IoT with Jared Wolff

claims.claim_text: Where the framework has no class API that matches a part exactly, the practical route is to implement the part against the nearest existing class API, as a real-time clock chip was implemented against Zephyr's timer API.
claims.quote_verbatim: they don't exactly have an API that matches it a hundred percent, but they did have a, I believe it was a timer API
claims.speaker: Jared Wolff
claims.episode_title: Cellular IoT with Jared Wolff

claims.claim_text: Because drivers conform to a class API, substituting a different part of the same class means writing a new driver against the same struct and changing a project configuration entry, with the application code left untouched.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I wanted to use a different RTC, I don't have to go through and recode everything. I can go to the data sheet and I can create another driver using that same kind of structure. And then I can just start using with my code and just, and then it's just a, a defined in my project file
claims.speaker: Jared Wolff
claims.episode_title: Cellular IoT with Jared Wolff

claims.claim_text: Nordic's Bluetooth stack ships as a precompiled binary, the soft device, that occupies a reserved region at the bottom of flash and a reserved portion of RAM and is reached only through a fixed API; the bootloader sits at the top of memory, and both regions must be placed in protected memory so application code cannot corrupt them.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's an API to this, like, this just chunk of memory. And, like, you just basically have to, like, preserve part of your flash and part of your RAM. And it's just going to run out of there
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Thermions Aren't A Thing

claims.claim_text: Consolidating several near-identical implementations into reusable modules forces the interfaces between them to be defined explicitly; the design work is deciding what abstraction lets a module connect to any other module rather than to one specific counterpart.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you make stuff modular, you start thinking about the API between them, the interfaces. How can I abstract the interface of this module to work with any other module that I want to connect it to
claims.speaker: Fredrik Kensander
claims.episode_title: High Current Power Supplies with Fredrik Kensander

claims.claim_text: Rather than inventing a hardware abstraction interface, a firmware team modelled its module interfaces on Zephyr's existing abstraction so the modules would carry over if the project later adopted the RTOS, using an established framework as a reference to implement against instead of iterating on a home-grown interface.
claims.quote_verbatim: we have something to follow and we don't invent it from, take something that works. Instead, if you try to invent it, you have to iterate over it to get it working. Here we have a reference. You can just implement like that reference
claims.speaker: Fredrik Kensander
claims.episode_title: High Current Power Supplies with Fredrik Kensander

claims.claim_text: The same team adopted the abstraction interface without adopting the RTOS underneath it, because the firmware is built around fixed-rate interrupts, roughly 1 kHz, 100 Hz and 10 Hz service loops plus a 37 kHz interrupt in the power module that must always be serviced, and an RTOS offered no benefit against that constraint.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have the 37 kilohertz interrupt. That's really important. That must always be served. So if you're going to put it in our R2OS, I don't see the immediate benefit
claims.speaker: Fredrik Kensander
claims.episode_title: High Current Power Supplies with Fredrik Kensander

claims.claim_text: Features of EDA tools that call distributor web APIs stop working in older tool releases once the distributors change those APIs; Altium's supplier search and manufacturing-parameter lookup broke in older versions for that reason, which removes staying on a known version as a strategy for avoiding an unfamiliar user interface.
claims.quote_verbatim: the supplier search and manufacturing parameters stuff is not working because DigiKey and others change their APIs. And so that's not supported in old versions of Altium
claims.episode_title: A Keyzermas Story

claims.claim_text: An FFT implemented in an embedded FPGA fabric was delivered to the customer as a bitstream plus a C API, so their software engineers called it as an ordinary function without knowing it ran in hardware; the benefit surfaced only as freed CPU cycles and memory, since the multiply-accumulate load moved off the processor.
claims.quote_verbatim: we actually created an FFT in the FPGA and we gave them the bit stream and we gave them an API in C that they could actually call. So from a software engineering point of view, done deal, right? Just call it an API. We take care of the fact that it's running in the FPGA
claims.speaker: Brian Faith
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains and Machine Learning with Brian Faith of QuickLogic

claims.claim_text: Some semiconductor and connector manufacturers publish their specification data through APIs, but many cannot, because growth by acquisition left the data unconsolidated; for those companies exposing an API is preceded by multi-year internal projects to get the data into a structured form at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: Some of the best chip companies and the best semiconductor companies and connector companies have APIs. But, like, the challenge that a lot of these companies have is that they don't have that data built up
claims.speaker: Natasha Baker
claims.episode_title: Footprints and Symbols with Natasha Baker

claims.claim_text: Consumer audio makers integrate with one of the three voice-assistant ecosystems, Google, Amazon or Apple, by implementing that vendor's APIs on a platform layer inside their product, which leaves the audio hardware unchanged and treats the assistant service as a required input path.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have APIs ready and all you need to do is implement those APIs and then you can play your music. You get your stream from somewhere and you can still build your device
claims.speaker: Remco Stoutjesdijk
claims.episode_title: High End Audio with Remco Stoutjesdijk

claims.claim_text: Pro audio uses OCA, an open control protocol, to make device control interfaces self-describing across manufacturers: a controller from one vendor plugged into a loudspeaker from another discovers that the device has a named gain control and can select which stream it listens to, removing the need to integrate a separate control scheme per vendor.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a protocol called OCA open control Alliance, where essentially now with you get the remote control from company a, you plug it into speaker from company B and it recognizes that the thing has a gain control and it has a name and you can, you can tell it which stream to listen to
claims.speaker: Remco Stoutjesdijk
claims.episode_title: High End Audio with Remco Stoutjesdijk

claims.claim_text: Supplier catalogue APIs allow live price and lead-time data to be presented at the moment of part selection, so the design engineer sees availability constraints while choosing rather than learning of them from procurement weeks or months later, after the design decision has been made and the context lost.
claims.quote_verbatim: increasing number of suppliers who are now digitizing their catalog and services and making APIs available, we do that. And so now engineers, when they're making those initial design decisions and part selections, have access to not only many more suppliers and part information, but real time did. And so if they see that the lead time or the prices don't meet their requirements, they can immediately take action and make, choose a different part or set different criteria in the initial design, right? Versus waiting weeks, months later to find out
claims.speaker: Michael Corr
claims.episode_title: Product Lifecycle Management with Michael Corr

claims.claim_text: Distributor APIs let a BOM management system raise obsolescence and lead-time alerts against parts already in a design, and then carry the substitution back through the CAD integration into an automatically populated change order.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can be notified much sooner that this part's the obsolete or lead time is no longer acceptable. And so then through our integrations, you can find an alternate, pop it into your design and then through our, our CAD integration quickly release it back into Duro. It auto-populates change order
claims.speaker: Michael Corr
claims.episode_title: Product Lifecycle Management with Michael Corr

claims.claim_text: FreeRTOS presents a deliberately minimal API, so building on it is a bottom-up exercise in which the developer writes most of the code; the reading burden appears once third-party libraries are brought in and their APIs and gotchas have to be understood.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's API is pretty minimal. So you're not really, I mean, if you're bringing in the exception of course is as soon as you start bringing in third-party libraries, you're reading a ton of code
claims.speaker: Brian Amos
claims.episode_title: Real Time Operating Systems with Brian Amos

claims.claim_text: The Joulescope JS220 driver was rewritten in C around a publish-subscribe API specifically so it could be bound to several languages, with a Python binding shipped against that same interface.
claims.quote_verbatim: we went to a total C driver. You know, like I said, we're all in on publish subscribe. We did that in C so we could actually bind to multiple languages, but we include a Python binding
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty
claims.episode_title: The Joulescope Upgrade with Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: Backwards compatibility across an instrument generation was preserved by shipping an adapter layer that presents the previous product's API on top of the new driver, so existing user scripts and the existing application keep working against new hardware while the new API is adopted incrementally.
claims.quote_verbatim: another layer of that, which wraps our previous API, the, the one that we use with the JS one 10. So as far as you know, you're running just like a JS one 10, except you're talking to a JS two 20. So you have the option of using the old API or the new one
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty
claims.episode_title: The Joulescope Upgrade with Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: Calling an existing upstream API is generally preferable to writing a driver, because upstream code has been tested and already exercised in shipped commercial products; the corresponding shift in higher-level frameworks is that a developer reads more code than they write, where bare-metal work is the reverse.
claims.quote_verbatim: I managed to just call this one API that was pretty much exactly the same, except that it's already, it's tested. It's, it's been in Zephyr upstream for years, which means that it's already used in commercial products
claims.speaker: Benjamin Cabe
claims.episode_title: Benjamin Cabé Nose Zephyr

claims.claim_text: Machine-control software can present one API across pick-and-place machines of different capability, with the per-machine configuration acting as a shim that adapts the differing control interfaces underneath; once a machine is tuned, the operator works against the abstraction rather than the machine.
claims.quote_verbatim: The configuration is just a, it's a shim layer to still have the same API with how do you control the thing? It's just different interface to actually control the machine underneath
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: Zephyr provides per-subsystem shell commands, covering operations such as an I2C bus scan, sensor reads and GPIO toggles, that are compiled into the image by enabling a configuration symbol; nearly every subsystem has an associated shell.
claims.quote_verbatim: zephyr has a lot of like built-in shells for like things like um talking i squared c you can do like an i squared c i squared c scan you can talk to sensors you can toggle gpios all the different things basically any feature that's in zephyr usually has a shell associated with it you can you can turn on with a symbol and then you can compile it in
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: It Works With Option Number 5

claims.claim_text: Writing a custom backend for the device shell and carrying it over a cloud remote-procedure-call channel makes a fielded device's local debug shell reachable from a browser over cellular, so GPIO toggles and serial readbacks can be performed remotely rather than requiring physical UART access.
claims.quote_verbatim: i wrote a remote procedure call that could accept a command called remote shell and then i could type in the shell command and then it would spit it back out as a as a return to the remote procedure call
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: It Works With Option Number 5

claims.claim_text: Distributor API access is tiered rather than uniform: DigiKey, Mouser and TI grant different levels of access depending on the account and the customer's standing, so an ERP integration reaches each one to a different depth.
claims.quote_verbatim: they don't always give you the full access. It depends upon who you are and where, where you're at
claims.speaker: Luke Beno
claims.episode_title: AI Tooling with Matt Liberty and Luke Beno

claims.claim_text: An API advertised as supporting a workflow may not deliver it in practice: a TI backlog account was taken partly to place orders through the vendor's API, but the ERP integration could not be made to work and was not supported, leaving a semi-manual upload path as the working method.
claims.quote_verbatim: I would need a way of placing an order through their API because that's how they advertised it. Well, they had recently just introduced a way you can kind of do this upload halfway in between thing. The integration with the ERP system, for some reason, I could not get working. They didn't really want to support me and uploading works fine
claims.speaker: Luke Beno
claims.episode_title: AI Tooling with Matt Liberty and Luke Beno
